newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Despite shipwrecks, death, Africans still seek Europe.
newsitem.headline: Despite shipwrecks, death, Africans still seek Europe.

text.p: Despite shipwrecks and deaths, the lure of Europe draws thousands of North Africans to perilous boats and, at best, an uncertain future as illegal immigrants.

The risks were again highlighted this week when Italian police picked up 40 would-be immigrants crammed in a motorboat. They were drifting at sea after eight days and said four of the group had died of cold and their bodies been pushed overboard.
Morocco and Tunisia are springboards not only for their own nationals seeking a better life but for Africans from countries like Mali and Niger who chance everything in the trek north.
From Morocco to Spain is about 14-km (eight miles). An estimated 4,000 illegal immigrants took that route in 1996, say Spanish and local police and press in northern Morocco.

From Tunisia, a favoured route is via the Italian island of Lampedusa, about 130-km (80-miles) from the nearest Tunisian fishing ports. In October, Italian police said nearly 1,500 people were detained on the island from January trying to enter Italy.

On Lampedusa, a senior officer in a report last month in Jeune Afrique magazine commented: "Makeshift boats come from Sfax and elsewhere with three times more people aboard than they should normally carry."
A helicopter and patrol boats ensure most are intercepted. But others drown, and nine graves mark bodies washed ashore.
Others try to go via Malta. On Thursday, Maltese and Italian aircraft were seeking survivors of a collision between two ships, one apparently carrying illegal immigrants.
But would-be immigrants shrug off the risks.

"At my age, when you lose hope of finding a job despite having a diploma, you automatically think of seeking another way out," a 27-year-old man, who gave his name as Omar, said in an interview with a North Moroccan local paper last year.

He had tried three times to get to Spain. "I was arrested twice as I left the boat which took us to near the Andalucian coast. The third time I got as far as Madrid where I was arrested by police and sent back to Morocco."
Moroccans who have succeeded and return on holiday with cash and in cars provide another catalyst by showing that at least for some the trip can succeed.
"Why not me?" asked Ahmed K., a 33-year-old jobless Moroccan from Tangier. "And above all when you live just 14-km from Spain, you can only try your luck."
He had tried five times and said he had seen youths throw themselves into the sea and vanish to try to avoid capture.
He was now working in "contraband" to try to save the 7,000 dirhams ($800) needed to pay for a sixth attempt.
Economic hardship is the driving force for most.

When late last year, a Moroccan fisherman Abdelaziz Fellah Boughaba was jailed for four years, his lawyer blamed his plight on government policy "which leads to the marginalisation of the young and to their misery."
Boughaba was the only survivor when his boat sank carrying 26 north Moroccans trying their luck for Spain. Each had paid 4,000 dirhams for the trip.

The European Union has been trying to staunch the flow of illegal immigrants from northern Morocco by pumping money into projects to provide jobs -- and an alternative crop to illegal cannabis which feeds drug traffickers heading to Europe.
($1 = 8.7 dirhams)
